# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 1 — The EMET Bible (Literal)

**Translator:** EMET | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus (ch 1-31) / P.Mich. 130 (ch 32+), Shepherd of Hermas 1 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_001_page_001.jpg

---

## Vision 1, Chapter 1

**1** The one who reared me sold me to a certain Rhoda in Rome. After many years I came to know her again, and I began to love her as a sister. **2** After some time I saw her bathing in the river Tiber, and I gave her my hand and helped her out of the river. Seeing her beauty I reasoned in my heart, saying, "How blessed would I be if I had a wife of such beauty and character." This only I thought in my heart — nothing further. **3** After some time, while I was traveling to Cumae and glorifying the creations of God — how great and marvelous and powerful they are — as I walked I fell into a sleep. **4** And a spirit took me and carried me through a certain trackless region, through which a man could not pass; for the place was precipitous and broken up by the water courses. **5** After crossing that river I came to the flat ground and knelt down and began to pray to the Lord and to confess my sins. **6** While I prayed, the heaven was opened and I saw the woman whom I had desired, greeting me from heaven, saying: "Greetings, Hermas." **7** And looking up at her I said, "Lady, what are you doing here?" And she answered me, "I was taken up in order to expose your sins before the Lord." **8** I said to her, "Are you now my accuser?" "No," she said, "but listen to the words I am about to say to you. God who dwells in the heavens and who created the things that are out of that which is not, and who multiplied and increased them for the sake of his holy church — **9** he is angry with you because you sinned against me." I answered and said to her, "Did I sin against you? In what way? When did I ever speak to you a dishonorable word? Did I not always regard you as a goddess? Did I not always reverence you as a sister? Why do you falsely accuse me, woman, of these wicked and unclean things?" **10** She laughed and said to me, "The desire of wickedness arose in your heart. Or does it not seem evil to you, for a righteous man to have a wicked desire arise in his heart? Yes," she said, "it is indeed sin, and a great one. For the righteous man aims at righteous things. As long then as he aims at righteous things and walks in them, he has a Lord in heaven. **11** But those who aim at wicked things and walk in them have a lord and a master who is wicked, ruinous, and treacherous. And walking between them, these people come to grief. **12** For when men who are holy and just have wicked desires, they bring sin upon themselves."

---

*EMET renders all terms with strict lexical precision. Greek hagnos = "holy/pure"; epithumia = "desire"; hamartia = "sin."*
